Hong Kong's Labour Department publishes statistics on work accidents and occupational diseases each
year. This notebook uses industrial accidents in factories, construction sites and restaurants from
1999 to 2025, occupational injuries in all kinds of work from 2006, occupational diseases, and
detail by industry and type of accident for 2024 and 2025. Read the module
[README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/hk-labour-osh-statistics/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name, ...) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           ...)
}

# Industrial accidents, occupational injuries, fatalities, workers and rates by year
trends <- read_module("tidy", "trends.csv")
# Confirmed occupational disease cases by disease
diseases <- read_module("tidy", "occupational_diseases.csv")
# 2024 and 2025: by industry, and by industry and type of accident
by_industry <- read_module("tidy", "by_industry_2024_2025.csv")
by_type <- read_module("tidy", "by_type_2024_2025.csv")
# The Labour Department's occupational health clinics
clinic <- read_module("tidy", "clinic_patients.csv")
services <- read_module("tidy", "health_services.csv")
```

Hong Kong counts accidents in two ways. **Industrial accidents** happen in industrial undertakings
(factories, construction sites, restaurants and some others), with rates per 1,000 workers.
**Occupational injuries** are all injuries at work with more than three days off, in every kind of
work, with rates per 1,000 employees. Industries were reclassified in 2009 (see the README).

# Part 1. The long view

```{r long-view}
trends |>
  filter(measure == "Industrial accident rate per 1,000 workers") |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = industry)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2008.5, linetype = "dashed") +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  labs(title = "Industrial accident rate per 1,000 workers",
       subtitle = "Dashed line: change of industry classification (HSIC 1.1 to 2.0)",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL)

trends |>
  filter(measure %in% c("Industrial accidents", "Industrial accident fatalities"),
         industry == "All industries", year %in% c(1999, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025)) |>
  select(year, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value)
```

**Questions**

1. By how much did the industrial accident rate in construction fall from 2006 to 2025? Which
   industry has had the highest rate in recent years?
2. The number of industrial accidents in all industries fell by more than 80% from 1999 to 2025.
   Give three possible explanations, at least one of which is not about safer work.
3. Why do the catering and food and beverage lines not join up in 2009? What would you need to
   compare them across the break?

# Part 2. Two ways of counting

```{r definitions}
trends |>
  filter((measure == "Industrial accidents" & industry == "All industries") |
           measure == "Occupational injuries", year >= 2006) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = measure)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  expand_limits(y = 0) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Industrial accidents and occupational injuries", x = NULL, y = NULL, colour = NULL)

trends |>
  filter(year >= 2016, measure %in% c("Industrial accident fatalities", "Work fatalities"),
         industry %in% c("All industries", "All economic activities")) |>
  select(year, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value)
```

**Questions**

1. About what share of occupational injuries are industrial accidents? Which kinds of work are
   counted as occupational injuries but not as industrial accidents?
2. Occupational injuries come from employers' reports under the Employees' Compensation Ordinance.
   What kinds of injuries or workers might not be reported?
3. Work fatalities include deaths in industrial undertakings and at other workplaces. About what
   share of work deaths happen outside industrial undertakings? Where might they happen?

# Part 3. Types of accident

```{r types}
by_type |>
  filter(statistic == "Industrial accidents", industry == "Total", accident_type != "Total",
         year == 2025) |>
  slice_max(cases, n = 10) |>
  ggplot(aes(cases, fct_reorder(accident_type, cases))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Industrial accidents by type, 2025", x = "Accidents", y = NULL)

by_type |>
  filter(statistic == "Industrial accidents", industry == "Construction",
         accident_type != "Total") |>
  group_by(accident_type) |>
  summarise(accidents = sum(cases), deaths = sum(fatalities)) |>
  filter(deaths > 0) |>
  arrange(desc(deaths))
```

**Questions**

1. What are the three most common types of industrial accident? Are they the same as the types
   that kill construction workers?
2. Falls of a person from height are a fraction of construction accidents but a large share of
   deaths. Why? List the hierarchy of controls for work at height, from most to least effective.
3. "Injured whilst lifting or carrying" is one of the most common types. What longer-term health
   problem is it linked to, and would these statistics capture it?

# Part 4. Industries

```{r industries}
by_industry |>
  filter(statistic == "Occupational injuries", industry != "Total") |>
  select(industry, year, cases) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = year, values_from = cases, names_prefix = "injuries_") |>
  arrange(desc(injuries_2025))

by_industry |>
  filter(statistic == "Occupational injuries", industry != "Total", year == 2025) |>
  ggplot(aes(fatalities, fct_reorder(industry, fatalities))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Deaths among occupational injuries, 2025", x = "Deaths", y = NULL)
```

# Part 5. Occupational diseases

```{r diseases}
top <- diseases |>
  filter(disease != "Total") |>
  group_by(disease) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  slice_max(cases, n = 5) |>
  pull(disease)

diseases |>
  filter(disease %in% top, !is.na(cases)) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, cases, colour = disease)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Confirmed occupational disease cases, five most common diseases", x = NULL,
       y = "Cases", colour = NULL)

diseases |>
  filter(disease %in% c("Total", "Occupational deafness", "Silicosis"), year >= 2016) |>
  select(year, disease, cases) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = disease, values_from = cases)
```

**Questions**

1. Which two diseases make up most cases? Both are caused by exposures that can be measured and
   controlled. Name the exposures and one control for each.
2. Occupational deafness cases jumped in 2011 and swing widely from year to year (78 in 2020, 394
   in 2021). Using the README, explain the jump in 2011, and suggest reasons for the swings that are
   not about noise exposure.
3. Silicosis and mesothelioma appear many years after exposure. What do this year's cases tell you
   about working conditions today?
